title: CSC3710 2026-08-20 — Course Map and the Vending-Machine DFA

questions.q: In this course, what is the difference between what a **grammar** does and what an **automaton** does with respect to a language?
choices: A grammar *generates* the strings of a language; an automaton *recognizes* (accepts or rejects) strings
A grammar recognizes strings; an automaton generates them
Both only translate programs into machine code
A grammar describes finite languages only; automata describe infinite ones
questions.explain: Grammars are rule systems that *generate* exactly the strings of a language (via derivations). Machines read an input string and decide membership, i.e. *recognize* the language. The course pairs each class of grammar with a matching class of machine.

questions.q: In the Chomsky hierarchy, which kind of machine recognizes the **context-free** languages (the class that describes a programming language's syntax)?
choices: Finite automata
Pushdown automata
Linear-bounded automata
Turing machines
questions.explain: Regular ↔ finite automata, context-free ↔ pushdown automata, context-sensitive ↔ linear-bounded automata, recursively enumerable ↔ Turing machines. A parser for Java's syntactic grammar is essentially a pushdown-automaton-style recognizer.

questions.q: Which language class does the vending-machine example belong to, and why?
choices: Regular, because a finite automaton recognizes it
Context-free, because it counts money
Recursively enumerable, because any computer program is
Context-sensitive, because the output depends on context
questions.explain: The vending machine is a DFA with 5 states. Any language recognized by a finite automaton is **regular**, the bottom rung of the hierarchy. Its fixed, finite memory (the running total, capped at $1+) is exactly what a finite automaton can hold.

questions.q: Each row of the Chomsky hierarchy (regular → context-free → context-sensitive → recursively enumerable) is strictly more powerful than the one below it: every regular language is context-free, but not every context-free language is regular.
questions.explain: The classes form a strict ladder. Each machine type can do everything the weaker one can, plus some languages it cannot. The course climbs from finite automata up to Turing machines in that order.

questions.q: You find a website whose notation for automata disagrees with the course textbook's. What does the course say to do?
choices: Follow the course's (textbook's) notation and vocabulary
Use whichever notation is more common online
Mix both, as long as you define symbols
Ask the TA to switch the course's notation
questions.explain: The instructor stressed that the course sticks to one notation and vocabulary, the textbook's. Online resources often use different symbols (e.g. ε vs λ) and some are simply wrong, so when they disagree, the course wins.

questions.q: Over an alphabet Σ, what is a **language**?
choices: Any subset of Σ\*, the set of all strings over Σ
Σ itself
Only an infinite set of strings
A set of rules that generates strings
questions.explain: A language is just a set of strings over Σ, i.e. any subset of Σ\*. It can be finite, infinite, or even empty. The *rules* that generate a language are a grammar, not the language itself.

questions.q: Which statements about the empty string are true in this course?
choices: It is written λ in Sudkamp and JFLAP
Many other books write it ε
It belongs to Σ\* for every alphabet Σ
It is a symbol of every alphabet
It has length 1
questions.explain: λ is the string with **no** symbols (length 0), not an alphabet symbol. Σ\* includes it by definition. Sudkamp and JFLAP write λ; many other texts use ε — another reason to stick to the course's notation.

questions.q: An alphabet may be an infinite set of symbols, as long as each string is finite.
questions.explain: An alphabet Σ is a **finite, nonempty** set of symbols, such as {0, 1} or the vending machine's {Q, H}. Strings are finite sequences over it; Σ\* (all strings) is infinite, but Σ itself is finite.

questions.q: A customer inserts a dime into the vending machine. How does the model treat it?
choices: It is outside the model: the alphabet is exactly {Q, H}
It moves the machine to a new $0.10 state
It is treated as λ
It sends the machine back to the initial state
questions.explain: The machine only 'understands' its alphabet symbols, Q and H. Dimes, pennies, bills and kicking the machine are simply not part of the model — the DFA describes how the machine is *supposed* to work on its defined inputs.

questions.q: Why is a grammar described as a **concise** description of a language?
choices: A finite set of rules pins down exactly which strings (possibly infinitely many) are in the language
It lists every string of the language explicitly
It explains what each program means
It is shorter than the compiler that uses it
questions.explain: The point is precision in few rules: the toy grammar's four lines generate exactly its six sentences, and about five pages of Java grammar decide, for *every* possible file, whether it is a Java program — an infinite set captured by a short formal object.

questions.q:
Using the toy grammar

```
<Sentence> → <Subject> <Verb> <Object>
<Subject>  → I | dogs
<Verb>     → like
<Object>   → me | dogs
```

which sentence **cannot** be derived?
choices: dogs like I
I like me
dogs like dogs
I like dogs
questions.explain: `I` is produced only by ⟨Subject⟩ → I, and the third position must come from ⟨Object⟩, which gives only `me` or `dogs`. So "dogs like I" is not in the language, even though it uses legal words — the *arrangement* violates the rules.

questions.q: How many distinct sentences does the toy grammar (⟨Sentence⟩ → ⟨Subject⟩ ⟨Verb⟩ ⟨Object⟩, ⟨Subject⟩ → I | dogs, ⟨Verb⟩ → like, ⟨Object⟩ → me | dogs) generate?
questions.explain: Each sentence is Subject Verb Object with 2 × 1 × 2 choices = **4**: I like me, I like dogs, dogs like me, dogs like dogs. (The lesson text says six, but the rules as written give four.) The point stands: a few rules describe the whole language exactly.

questions.q: What does a **parser** do in a compiler?
choices: Checks the token stream against the language's grammar and builds a parse tree; invalid input gives a syntax error
Translates bytecode into machine code
Checks that variable types match
Runs the program to see if it crashes
questions.explain: The parser is the compiler's front-end gatekeeper: it is built from the grammar and decides whether the source is syntactically valid. Valid programs go on to later phases (type checking, code generation); invalid ones produce syntax errors.

questions.q: What happens to the Java statement `int x = "hello";`?
choices: It parses successfully and is rejected later by the type checker
It is rejected by the parser as a syntax error
It is rejected by the lexer
It compiles and runs, printing hello
questions.explain: It has the syntactic shape of a declaration (type, identifier, `=`, expression, `;`), so it matches the grammar. Parsing checks **syntax only**; assigning a String to an int is caught by type checking, a later compiler phase.

questions.q: In the Java Language Specification, the **lexical** grammar groups characters into tokens and the **syntactic** grammar arranges tokens into programs. Which language classes / machines fit each?
choices: Lexical: regular (finite automata); syntactic: context-free (pushdown automata)
Lexical: context-free; syntactic: regular
Both are regular
Both require Turing machines
questions.explain: Token patterns (identifiers, literals, keywords) are regular expressions, recognizable by finite automata. Nested structures like `if ( Expression ) Statement` need context-free grammars, recognized by pushdown automata.

questions.q: Because the Java grammar is a complete definition of the language, reading it is a good way to learn how to program in Java.
questions.explain: The grammar says exactly *what is legal*, not *what it means* or *how to use it well*. The instructor stressed you would not learn Java from those five pages, even though they completely define its syntax.

questions.q: Is your laptop a Turing machine?
choices: Only under the idealization that memory is unlimited (more storage can always be added); strictly, it is a huge finite machine
Yes, unconditionally, because it runs any program
No, it is only a pushdown automaton
No, because it is digital and Turing machines are analog
questions.explain: With fixed memory a laptop has finitely many configurations (e.g. 16 GB → at most 2^(2^37)), so strictly it is a finite automaton. We model it as a Turing machine by assuming memory is unbounded — 'you can always add another disk'.

questions.q: Why is it reasonable to model a computer as a Turing machine even though no computer has infinite memory?
choices: A TM only needs *unbounded* memory: at any moment it has used finitely many cells but can always get another
Real computers secretly have infinite memory via virtual memory
Turing machines have a fixed-size tape too
Because RAM is random access, like a tape
questions.explain: A Turing machine's tape has no fixed limit, but any run uses only finitely many cells at each step. 'Just add another disk' plays exactly that role, and the finite-automaton view of a real computer is useless in practice.

questions.q: Which are parts of a Turing machine?
choices: A finite set of states (finite control)
An unbounded tape of cells
A read/write head that moves one cell left or right per step
A finite table of rules
An infinite set of states
questions.explain: A TM has a *finite* control like a DFA, plus an unbounded tape as memory, and a head that reads, writes, moves and changes state according to a finite rule table. The states are finite; only the tape is unbounded.

questions.q: Why is the Church–Turing thesis called a *thesis* rather than a theorem?
choices: It equates an informal idea (effectively computable) with a formal one (Turing-computable), so it cannot be proved
It has been disproved by quantum computers
It is an open problem with a $1M prize
It is only true for finite automata
questions.explain: You cannot formally prove that an informal notion equals a formal definition. The evidence is empirical: every model proposed (lambda calculus, recursive functions, register machines, programming languages) computes exactly the same functions.

questions.q: Which of the following is actually one of the Clay Millennium Prize Problems ($1M)?
choices: P vs NP
The Church–Turing thesis
Whether quantum computers beat Turing machines
The Traveling Salesman Problem's decidability
questions.explain: The lecture attributed the prize to proving the Church–Turing thesis, but the lesson corrects this: the $1M problem is **P vs NP**, a question of *efficiency*, not computability. For exams, file the prize under P vs NP.

questions.q: It has been proven that no model of computation more powerful than the Turing machine can exist.
questions.explain: No one has found a more powerful model, and every reasonable proposed model is equivalent, but nobody has *proved* nothing stronger exists. That belief is the (unprovable) Church–Turing thesis.

questions.q: A quantum computer can solve some problems that no Turing machine can solve.
questions.explain: Any quantum computation can be simulated classically (possibly exponentially slower), so quantum computers compute exactly the Turing-computable functions. 'More powerful' can only mean *faster* on some problems (BQP), never a larger set of solvable problems.

questions.q: The Traveling Salesman Problem is described as **computable but intractable**. What does that mean?
choices: An algorithm always finds the answer, but its running time explodes for large inputs (no polynomial algorithm known)
No algorithm can ever solve it
It can be solved quickly but not checked
It is only solvable on quantum computers
questions.explain: Brute force ('try every tour') always terminates with the correct answer, so TSP is computable (decidable). But the number of tours grows factorially, so large instances could take thousands to millions of years — intractable.

questions.q: For a TSP with **7** cities, how many distinct round trips must brute force check, using (n − 1)!/2?
questions.explain: (7 − 1)!/2 = 720/2 = **360**. Fix the start city, order the remaining 6 (6! = 720), then divide by 2 because each loop can be traveled in either direction.

questions.q: In the TSP tour count (n − 1)!/2, why is (n − 1)! divided by 2?
choices: Each round trip can be traveled in two directions and counts as the same tour
Half the tours are invalid
Only half the cities are visited
Because the start city is fixed
questions.explain: Fixing the start city gives (n − 1)! orderings of the rest; each tour and its reverse have the same length, so they are one tour, halving the count.

questions.q: Which pairings of question and area are correct?
choices: Church–Turing thesis — computability (what can be computed at all)
P vs NP — complexity (what can be computed efficiently)
Quantum computers' possible advantage — complexity (speed)
TSP being hard — computability (it cannot be solved)
questions.explain: Computability asks whether a problem can be solved at all; complexity asks how fast. Quantum computers and TSP both live on the complexity side: TSP *is* solvable, just slowly; quantum computers may be faster but solve nothing new.

questions.q: How is the TSP tied to the P vs NP question?
choices: Its decision version ('is there a tour shorter than x?') is NP-complete, so a polynomial-time algorithm for it would resolve P vs NP
It was proven to be undecidable
It is in P, so P = NP
Quantum computers solve it in polynomial time, proving P ≠ NP
questions.explain: NP-complete problems are the hardest in NP; a polynomial algorithm for any one would give one for all, showing P = NP. Even quantum algorithms (Grover-style) give only a quadratic speedup on TSP-like search.

questions.q: What makes a finite automaton **deterministic**?
choices: Every state has exactly one outgoing transition for every input symbol
It has exactly one final state
It has no self-loops
Every state has at least one outgoing transition
questions.explain: Deterministic means from any state, for any symbol, the next state is fully determined: exactly one arrow per symbol from every state. Formally, δ : Q × Σ → Q is a *total* function. Self-loops and multiple final states are allowed.

questions.q: A DFA has 7 states and alphabet {a, b, c}. How many transitions must it have?
questions.explain: A DFA needs exactly one transition for each (state, symbol) pair: |Q| × |Σ| = 7 × 3 = **21**. The vending machine has 5 × 2 = 10.

questions.q: A partly drawn vending machine has these outgoing arrows: $0.00 (Q, H), $0.25 (Q, H), $0.50 (Q, H), $0.75 (Q only), $1.00+ (none). How many arrows are missing before it is a DFA?
questions.explain: Each of the 5 states needs 2 arrows (10 total); 7 are present. Missing: $0.75 —H→ $1.00+, $1.00+ —Q→ $0.25, $1.00+ —H→ $0.50. That was exactly the class's half-built state.

questions.q: Why is $0.00 (the initial state) **not** made the final state of the vending machine?
choices: Plugging the machine in would already put it in the 'bottle dispensed' state — free water; formally λ would be accepted
A DFA may not have its initial state final
The machine would become nondeterministic
JFLAP cannot mark an initial state as final
questions.explain: The initial state is where the machine sits on plug-in. If it were final, no coins at all would count as a purchase (unplug/replug for endless water). Formally, the empty string λ would be accepted. DFAs *may* make q₀ final in general — it's just wrong for this design.

questions.q: How does the vending-machine DFA model 'the next coin starts a new count from zero' without returning to $0.00?
choices: $1.00+ is given the same outgoing transitions as $0.00: Q → $0.25 and H → $0.50
$1.00+ has a λ-transition back to $0.00
$1.00+ has self-loops on Q and H
The machine automatically resets after reaching a final state
questions.explain: Copying $0.00's outgoing arrows makes $1.00+ behave as if the count were zero, while never re-entering the initial state. DFAs have no λ-moves and no automatic resets — they move only when reading a symbol.

questions.q: In the vending machine, where does $0.75 go on input **H** (total $1.25)?
choices: $1.00+ (no change given, and '$1 or more' is enough)
A new $1.25 state
Back to $0.25 to give change
$0.75 (self-loop)
questions.explain: The machine gives no change and only needs the total to reach or exceed $1, so both Q and H from $0.75 go to $1.00+. JFLAP draws these two transitions as one arrow labeled Q, H.

questions.q: After entering the final state $1.00+, the DFA automatically moves back to the initial state without reading any input.
questions.explain: A DFA moves only when it reads an input symbol, and each move consumes the symbol (the coin is 'eaten'). There are no free moves; λ-transitions appear only later, in NFAs. The machine stays in $1.00+ until the next coin.

questions.q: For the vending machine as M = (Q, Σ, δ, q₀, F), which are correct?
choices: Σ = {Q, H}

questions.q: You redesign the machine for a **$1.25** bottle (same coins, no change, reset after each bottle), with states $0.00, $0.25, $0.50, $0.75, $1.00, $1.25+. How many transitions does the DFA have?
questions.explain: 6 states × 2 symbols = **12**. The new $1.00 state goes to $1.25+ on both Q and H ($1.50 with no change), $0.75 —H→ $1.25+, and $1.25+ copies $0.00's arrows (Q → $0.25, H → $0.50).

questions.q: A DFA with more states than necessary for its language is incorrect.
questions.explain: For the same requirements, many correct machines exist, and you can always use more states than needed. Such a design is correct, just not the smallest. (There is a unique minimal DFA up to renaming; the 5-state vending machine already is minimal.)

questions.q: In JFLAP, $0.75 has transitions on both Q and H to $1.00+. How is this drawn, and how should you count it when checking determinism?
choices: One arrow with stacked labels Q and H; count the labels (2 transitions)
Two separate arrows; count arrows
One arrow; it counts as 1 transition
JFLAP refuses to draw two transitions between the same states
questions.explain: JFLAP merges transitions between the same pair of states into one arrow with stacked labels. When verifying 'one per symbol per state', count labels, not arrows.

questions.q: Trace the vending machine on `QHQH`. Where does it end, and is the string accepted?
choices: Ends at $0.50; rejected (1 bottle dispensed along the way)
Ends at $1.00+; accepted
Ends at $0.75; rejected
Ends at $0.50; accepted because a bottle was dispensed
questions.explain: $0.00 →Q $0.25 →H $0.75 →Q $1.00+ (bottle) →H $0.50. Acceptance depends only on where the machine is after the **last** symbol, so it is rejected even though a bottle came out.

questions.q: When does a DFA accept a string?
choices: When it is in a final state after reading the last symbol
Whenever it passes through a final state
When it reads every symbol without getting stuck
When it returns to the initial state
questions.explain: Start in q₀, follow δ for each symbol, and accept iff the state after the *last* symbol is in F. Passing through a final state mid-string (e.g. `HHQ`) does not make the string accepted.

questions.q: Which strings does the vending-machine DFA accept?
choices: `HQH`
`QQQQ`
`HHHH`
`QQQ`
`HHQ`
λ
questions.explain: `HQH`: $0.50 → $0.75 → $1.00+ (paid $1.25). `QQQQ`: ends at $1.00+. `HHHH`: two purchases in a row, ends at $1.00+. `QQQ` ends at $0.75, `HHQ` at $0.25 (a new purchase started), and λ stays at $0.00 (not final).

questions.q: How many strings of length 3 over {Q, H} does the vending-machine DFA accept?
questions.explain: `QQH`, `QHQ`, `HQQ` (exactly $1.00) and `QHH`, `HQH` ($1.25) end in $1.00+. `QQQ` ends at $0.75, `HHQ` at $0.25, `HHH` at $0.50 — a bottle came out after `HH` but the run ends mid-purchase.

questions.q: On input `QQQQQ`, how many bottles are dispensed, and is the string accepted?
choices: 1 bottle; rejected (ends at $0.25)
1 bottle; accepted
0 bottles; rejected
2 bottles; accepted
questions.explain: $0.00 → $0.25 → $0.50 → $0.75 → $1.00+ (bottle 1) → $0.25. Bottles = number of times the run *enters* $1.00+; acceptance only checks the final state.

questions.q: Which best describes L(M), the language of the vending-machine DFA?
choices: Coin sequences made of one or more complete purchases in a row — i.e. whose last coin completes a purchase
All coin sequences totaling at least $1
All coin sequences totaling exactly $1
Coin sequences containing at least one purchase anywhere
questions.explain: Because $1.00+ behaves like $0.00 for the next coin, L(M) = P P\* where P is the set of 8 purchases (QQQQ, QQH, QHQ, HQQ, HH, QQQH, QHH, HQH). `HHQ` totals $1.25 but is rejected, ruling out the 'at least $1' options.

questions.q: A **purchase** is a coin sequence whose running total first reaches $1 or more on its last coin. How many distinct purchases are there with quarters and half dollars?
questions.explain: Exactly $1.00: QQQQ, QQH, QHQ, HQQ, HH (5). Overshoot to $1.25 on a final half dollar: QQQH, QHH, HQH (3). Total **8**.

questions.q: Which single string of length 2 does the vending-machine DFA accept? (Use Q and H.)
questions.explain: Only two half dollars reach $1.00 in two coins: $0.00 →H $0.50 →H $1.00+. Any string with a Q in it totals at most $0.75.
